origin_category: new_teaching_material: independent translation of the exact source, reconciled with checked lexical evidence

segments.model: Every high honour here in the world is beset by dangers; the greater the worldly distinctions, the fiercer the dangers.
segments.essential_meaning: High worldly status brings danger; the second pair states a proportion, not merely equality.
alternatives: high office / high position for high honour
the greater the worldly dignities, the greater or stronger the dangers

segments.model: Thus, from that, we can recognize and understand the examples.
segments.essential_meaning: The examples are the accusative object of both infinitives. From/by that refers separately to the preceding proposition.
segments.diagnosis: Do not make examples the dative complement of be or collapse the distinct phrases into from these examples.

segments.model: The tree, then, which grows in the woodland so that it towers above all the other trees and spreads itself out—when suddenly a storm and the strong wind arise, it is shaken and battered more violently than the rest of the forest.
segments.essential_meaning: The tallest spreading tree is more exposed to the storm; tree is the actor of spreading and the patient of shaking. Storm and wind are the coordinated subjects of gestęnt.
alternatives: blows up / sets in for arises
segments.diagnosis: Keep the delayed main clause and resumptive pronoun intelligible. The rest of the forest does not mean a different forest.

segments.model: It is likewise with the high cliffs and crags: when they tower far above the rest of the earth, they then suddenly begin to fall and crash very violently to the ground.
segments.essential_meaning: The next example continues the same comparison. Both infinitives depend on begin; the pronouns refer to cliffs and crags.
alternatives: to the earth for to the ground
fall and collapse for fall and crash
segments.note: Crags is Cook’s probable contextual interpretation of torrum; the source help retains that qualification.

segments.model: Likewise with the high mountains and hills, which stand high above the whole world: nevertheless they suffer the penalty of their eminence, in that they are often chastised and afflicted by fire from heaven and struck by thunderbolts.
segments.essential_meaning: Height entails punishment: the passive clause explains what that penalty is. Lightning/thunderbolts is the checked sense of līegum.
alternatives: harried and crushed for chastised and afflicted
segments.diagnosis: Do not turn the explanatory clause into a purpose for the mountains. The genitive ealdordōmes depends on penalty.

segments.model: So the high powers here in the world collapse and fall and come to ruin, and the riches of this world turn to sorrow, and these earthly wonders come to nothing.
segments.essential_meaning: The conclusion transfers the natural examples to worldly power and wealth. Of this world is genitive dependent on riches; riches and wonders are subjects of their own verbs.
alternatives: those in high power / potentates for high powers
come to naught for come to nothing
segments.diagnosis: Keep the plural subjects and the concluding result expressions; do not make the riches the object of the preceding falling verbs.

translation_note: The natural English dash and colon clarify the long argument; they are translation punctuation and do not alter the separate diplomatic Old English text. No prior-course solution was used as the translation source.
